t: Can You Eat Your Favorite Candy on Your Favorite Day? - Prefix Sums and Feasibility Windows
o: Candy types must be consumed in order: you cannot touch type i until every candy of type i-1 is gone, you eat at least one candy every day starting at day 0, and you never exceed dailyCap candies in a day. Each query asks whether some legal schedule lets you eat a candy of type favoriteType on day favoriteDay. Look at candiesCount = [7,4,5,3,8]: query [0,2,2] is true because with cap 2 per day you can still be nibbling type 0 on day 2; query [4,2,4] is false because types 0..3 hold 19 candies and two days at cap 4 clear at most 8, so type 4 is unreachable; query [2,13,1000000000] is true because types 0..1 hold only 11 candies - even eating one per day you reach type 2 by day 11 - while types 0..2 total 16, so day 13 still lies inside type 2. Only the prefix sums around favoriteType matter: pre[t] is a barrier of predecessors you must finish, and pre[t+1] - 1 is the last day a type-t candy can still exist. On day d you have eaten somewhere between d candies (the one-per-day minimum) and d * cap candies, so the query is feasible exactly when that interval reaches into [pre[t], pre[t+1] - 1]. Note favoriteDay and dailyCap both reach 10^9, so the product reaches 10^18 - beyond 32-bit range and beyond exact double precision in JavaScript.
k: Feasibility is a window test on the day index: type t is edible on day d iff ceil(pre[t] / cap) <= d <= pre[t + 1] - 1.
The lower bound comes from the must-eat-one-per-day rule (you cannot be forced past type t too early); the upper bound from capacity (d days give at most d * cap candies to clear pre[t]).
favoriteDay * dailyCap can hit 10^18: use 64-bit integers in Java/C++, or avoid the multiplication entirely via ceiling division.

a.n: Approach 1: Direct Interval Test with Big Products
a.i: Translate the rules literally. By day d you could have eaten as many as d * cap candies - reaching type t requires finishing its pre[t] predecessors first. Conversely, even eating the bare minimum of d candies during days 0..d-1 must not have exhausted type t, which needs d < pre[t + 1]. One prefix-sum array plus an O(1) conjunction per query.
s: Build prefix sums pre where pre[t] = total candies of types 0..t-1.
For each query check pre[t] <= day * cap (enough time and capacity to arrive).
Check day + 1 <= pre[t + 1] (type t is not exhausted before the favorite day).
Output the conjunction of both checks.
a.t: O(n + q) - one prefix pass, constant work per query.

a.n: Approach 2: Earliest/Latest Day Window via Ceiling Division
a.i: Reframe the test as computing the set of days on which type t is edible. The earliest arrival day is ceil(pre[t] / cap): full-capacity days needed to clear the predecessors. The latest is pre[t + 1] - 1: the last day fewer than all of types 0..t are gone. The answer is simply whether favoriteDay falls inside [earliest, latest], and computing earliest by ceiling division keeps every intermediate value near 10^10, so no wide integer types are required at all.
s: earliest = ceil(pre[t] / cap), computed as (pre[t] + cap - 1) div cap.
Answer true iff earliest <= favoriteDay <= latest.
a.t: O(n + q) - identical structure; each query is O(1).

w: Go with the window formulation: deriving 'earliest day I could possibly arrive' and 'latest day the type still exists' is the crisp way to present it, and ceiling division sidesteps the overflow landmine completely. Pitfalls: dropping the must-eat-one-per-day rule - it supplies the lower bound that kills queries like [4, 2, 4]; comparing day * cap in 32-bit ints in Java/C++ (silent overflow produces wrong answers); and trusting JavaScript Numbers for products near 10^18, where precision loss silently corrupts comparisons - use the division form or BigInt. Follow-ups: minimize the number of days to finish all candies, support per-day varying caps (prefix sums of capacities plus binary search), or count how many days each type is edible.
